reason: The sources provide 16 detailed, multi-sourced claims covering Puyi's life from child emperor to gardener, including specific dates, names, and quotes.
story: Puyi's life was a tragic sequence of falls from heights few can imagine. Crowned at age two, he was treated as a living god in the Forbidden City, where his every sadistic whim was indulged while he remained a virtual prisoner of ancient etiquette. In 1912, he was forced to abdicate, ending 2,000 years of imperial rule and beginning a decades-long descent into political irrelevance. He spent his adulthood as a pawn, eventually serving as the puppet emperor of Japanese-occupied Manchukuo. After the war, he was captured by Soviet troops and later imprisoned by the Chinese Communist Party for 'reeducation.' In a final irony, the man who once owned all of China was released in 1959 to live as a humble citizen. He spent his remaining years tending plants as a gardener at the Beijing Botanical Gardens, near the very palaces where he had once been worshipped as the Son of Heaven.
angle: The former 'Son of Heaven' who once owned all of China ended his life as a quiet citizen working as a gardener in the city he once ruled.

claims.claim: Puyi was the last emperor of China.

evidence.quote: Puyi (Chinese: 溥儀; pinyin: Pǔ Yí; Wade–Giles: P'u-i; 7 February 1906 – 17 October 1967) was the last emperor of China
the last emperor of China, a six year old boy named Puyi, formally abdicated the throne

claims.claim: Puyi became emperor in 1908 when he was nearly three years old.

evidence.quote: Puyi became emperor at the age of 2 years 10 months and 25 days in December 1908
Puyi was crowned Emperor of China in 1908, aged just 2 years and 10 months.

claims.claim: As a child emperor, Puyi was known for his cruelty and frequently had his eunuchs beaten.

evidence.quote: frequently had them beaten for small transgressions.
He became cruel, taking pleasure in having his eunuchs whipped regularly

claims.claim: The abdication established the Republic of China as the successor to the Qing dynasty.

evidence.quote: Imperial Edict established the First Republic of China as the immediate successor state to the Qing dynasty
What replaced it was the Republic of China, a fragile experiment in modern governance

claims.claim: Following his abdication, Puyi was allowed to retain his imperial title and continue living in the Forbidden City.

evidence.quote: the Articles of Favorable Treatment allowed him to retain his imperial title and remain in the Forbidden City.
the imperial family was granted a generous settlement: they could continue living in the Forbidden City, retain their titles

claims.claim: Scottish scholar Reginald Johnston was hired as Puyi's tutor in the Forbidden City.

evidence.quote: the Scottish scholar and diplomat Reginald Johnston arrived in the Forbidden City to serve as Puyi's tutor.
The teenage Puyi was given an English tutor, Sir Reginald Johnston

claims.claim: Puyi married the aristocrat Wanrong in 1922.

evidence.quote: On 21 October 1922, Puyi's wedding to Princess Wanrong began
The pair were betrothed in March 1922 and married that autumn.

claims.claim: Soviet troops captured Puyi in 1945 at the end of the Second Sino-Japanese War.

evidence.quote: At the end of the Second Sino-Japanese War in 1945, he was captured by the Soviet Red Army
With the Japanese surrender in 1945, his dreams of empire were dashed, and the chastened Emperor was trundled off by advancing Soviet troops

claims.claim: Puyi testified at the Tokyo War Crimes Tribunal.

evidence.quote: testified at the Tokyo War Crimes Tribunal in 1946
He subsequently testified at the Tokyo War Trials in an attempt to defend himself
he died without issue in 1967.
died, unmourned, of cancer at a Beijing hospital in 1967

disputed: Post-release occupation: Source S6 mentions Puyi worked as a street sweeper, while S1 and S3 specify he was a gardener and handyman at the Botanical Gardens.
Repatriation date: Source S1 states Puyi was repatriated to China in 1950, while S6 states it occurred in 1949.
His attitude toward his later life: S3 describes him as solemn and perhaps regretful, while S6 emphasizes his epiphany and kindness in his final years.
